name: ATLAS
aliases: Ambulatory Treatments for Leakage Associated with Stress Incontinence
question: For women seeking nonsurgical treatment of stress-predominant urinary incontinence, how do a continence pessary, behavioral therapy, and their combination compare?

design.blinding: Participants and interventionists unblinded; examination and telephone outcome assessors blinded

arms.label: Behavioral therapy: pelvic-floor muscle training and continence strategies
physician- or nurse-fitted continence ring or dish pessary

design.population: Women aged at least 18 years with stress-only or stress-predominant mixed urinary incontinence seeking nonsurgical care.
design.description: Nine-site, assessor-blinded, three-arm randomized superiority trial

verdictNote: Behavioral therapy improved symptom bother, not global improvement; combination failed its superiority rule.
takeaway: In women with stress-predominant incontinence, behavioral pelvic-floor therapy produced fewer bothersome stress symptoms than a fitted continence pessary at three months, but global improvement did not significantly differ. Adding a pessary to behavioral therapy did not meet the prespecified superiority rule.

reports.label: Continence pessary fitting analysis
reports.citation: Nager CW, Richter HE, Nygaard I, et al. "Incontinence pessaries: size, POPQ measures, and successful fitting." *Int Urogynecol J.* 2009;20(9):1023-1028. doi:10.1007/s00192-009-0866-1
reports.followUp: Fitting visits within the ATLAS treatment period

results.measure: Final recorded fitting outcome in pessary-assigned arms
results.note: 235/255 women (92%) with a recorded final fit outcome were fitted; the paper describes 266 assigned to the pessary-containing arms.

results.measure: Association of POP-Q measurements with final pessary diameter
results.note: Total vaginal length, point C, and point D did not predict final diameter; mean vaginal length was 9.6 cm with successful fit versus 8.8 cm with unsuccessful fit (P<0.01).

delivery.label: Fitting protocol and device types
delivery.value: A trained nurse, nurse practitioner, or physical therapist selected a continence ring or dish; fit required a finger between device and vaginal wall and retention on standing, coughing, and straining. Among successful fittings, 122 used a ring and 113 a dish.
delivery.locator: Methods, fitting protocol; Results, fitting success paragraph

reports.label: Primary trial and 12-month outcomes
reports.dateLocator: PubMed and journal specify March 2010; day not verified
reports.citation: Richter HE, Burgio KL, Brubaker L, et al. "Continence pessary compared with behavioral therapy or combined therapy for stress incontinence: a randomized controlled trial." *Obstet Gynecol.* 2010;115(3):609-617. doi:10.1097/AOG.0b013e3181d055d4
reports.followUp: Primary outcomes at 3 months; repeated assessments at 6 and 12 months

results.measure: 3-month much or very much better; behavioral minus pessary risk difference in percentage points
results.note: Intention to treat; adjusted comparison; final PGI-I alpha 0.0492 after interim analysis.

results.measure: 3-month PFDI UDI-stress success; behavioral minus pessary risk difference in percentage points
results.note: No symptoms or symptoms rated not at all/somewhat bothersome on all stress items; intention to treat.

results.measure: 3-month PGI-I; combined therapy had to exceed both single treatments
results.note: Combined versus pessary P=0.02; combined versus behavioral P=0.49. One randomized combination participant was ineligible and excluded.
results.locator: Methods, Statistical Analysis; Table 3 and footnote 2

results.endpoint: Combined therapy: no bothersome stress symptoms
results.measure: 3-month PFDI UDI-stress success; combined therapy had to exceed both single treatments
results.note: Combined versus pessary P=0.05; combined versus behavioral P=0.42.
results.locator: Methods, Statistical Analysis; Table 3 and footnotes 4-5

results.measure: 3-month satisfied or somewhat satisfied; behavioral minus pessary risk difference in percentage points
results.note: Behavioral-versus-pessary P=0.03 in Table 3 footnote 8 and Results; abstract prints P=0.02.
results.locator: Table 3 and footnote 8; Results paragraph after Table 3

results.endpoint: At least 75% fewer weekly incontinence episodes
results.note: No significant between-group differences; 68/146 is 46.6% by arithmetic, although Table 3 prints 46.7%.

results.endpoint: Patient Global Impression of Improvement at 12 months
results.measure: 12-month much or very much better; intention to treat
results.note: No statistically significant between-group difference at 12 months.

results.endpoint: No bothersome stress-incontinence symptoms at 12 months
results.measure: 12-month PFDI UDI-stress success; intention to treat
results.note: No statistically significant between-group difference at 12 months.

harms.label: Vaginal discharge by 3 months
harms.note: Percentages only in report; 7% overall reported yeast infection; no vaginal erosions reported.

harms.label: Unexpected urologic adverse events
harms.note: Ten events overall: seven urinary tract infections, two possible infections, and one possible retention event.

delivery.label: Behavioral intervention
delivery.value: Four standardized visits about two weeks apart over eight weeks, delivered by trained nurses, nurse practitioners, or physical therapists; individualized daily pelvic-floor exercises and continence strategies followed by home maintenance.

delivery.label: Continence pessary fitting
delivery.value: Physician or nurse fitted a continence ring or dish; up to three fitting visits at one- to two-week intervals were allowed.

delivery.label: Withdrawal at 3 months
delivery.note: Twelve pessary-arm withdrawals were attributed to inadequate fit.

delivery.label: Continued treatment at one year
delivery.value: 45% still reported pessary use; 57% still reported pelvic-floor exercises.
delivery.note: The report gives percentages without adherence denominators.

reports.label: Pelvic symptom and quality-of-life analysis
reports.dateLocator: PubMed gives March-April 2012 issue; online day not verified
reports.citation: Kenton K, Barber M, Wang L, et al. "Pelvic floor symptoms improve similarly after pessary and behavioral treatment for stress incontinence." *Female Pelvic Med Reconstr Surg.* 2012;18(2):118-121. doi:10.1097/SPV.0b013e31824a021d

results.endpoint: Change in pelvic symptom distress and condition-specific quality of life
results.note: 295 women were randomized to these two arms; no statistically significant between-group difference in the analyzed urinary, prolapse, or colorectal symptom and impact scores.

reports.label: Predictors of success and satisfaction
reports.dateLocator: PubMed gives July 2012 issue; online day not verified
reports.citation: Schaffer J, Nager CW, Xiang F, et al. "Predictors of success and satisfaction of nonsurgical therapy for stress urinary incontinence." *Obstet Gynecol.* 2012;120(1):91-97. doi:10.1097/AOG.0b013e31825a6de7

results.endpoint: Prior incontinence surgery and symptom success
results.measure: Adjusted odds of 3-month UDI-stress success, no prior surgery versus prior surgery
results.note: Adjusted association among 445 analyzed women across all three treatment arms; no significant treatment interaction.

results.measure: Adjusted odds of 3-month satisfaction, fewer than 14 versus at least 14 episodes per week
results.note: Adjusted association among 445 analyzed women across all three treatment arms; no significant treatment interaction.
